questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol{x}^{(k)}$ be points of a linear program and $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k$ weights. Under which hypothesis is $\boldsymbol{x}=\sum_j\alpha_j\boldsymbol{x}^{(j)}$ guaranteed to be optimal?
options: All $\boldsymbol{x}^{(j)}$ are feasible, and $\alpha_j\ge0$ with $\sum_j\alpha_j=1$.
All $\boldsymbol{x}^{(j)}$ are optimal, and $\alpha_j\ge0$ with $\sum_j\alpha_j=1$.
All $\boldsymbol{x}^{(j)}$ are optimal corners, with any real weights $\alpha_j$.
Each $\boldsymbol{x}^{(j)}$ is optimal for some LP, and $\alpha_j\ge0$ with $\sum_j\alpha_j=1$.

questions.question: Two optimal solutions $\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)},\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}$ of an LP are combined as $\alpha_1\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}+\alpha_2\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}$. Which pair of weights is always allowed by the proposition on convex combinations?
options: $\alpha_1=1.2$ and $\alpha_2=-0.2$
$\alpha_1=0.5$ and $\alpha_2=0.6$
$\alpha_1=0.4$ and $\alpha_2=0.4$
$\alpha_1=0.3$ and $\alpha_2=0.7$

questions.question: Two optimal solutions $\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)},\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}$ of an LP satisfy every constraint $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\le b$. Why does $\alpha\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}+(1-\alpha)\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}$ with $0\le\alpha\le1$ also satisfy it?
options: The objective value is unchanged, so the constraints still hold.
Both points are corners, and corners satisfy every constraint.
Nonnegativity of the variables makes every constraint hold.
Its left side is a weighted average of two values at most $b$.

questions.question: An LP has two distinct optimal corner points. How many optimal solutions does it have?
options: Exactly two: the two optimal corner points themselves
Infinitely many, all on the segment between them
Exactly three: the two corners and their midpoint
Only the corners, since LP optima lie at corners

questions.question: For optimal solutions $\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}$ and $\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}$ of an LP, the combination $\boldsymbol{x}(\alpha)=\alpha\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}+(1-\alpha)\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}$ is formed. Which point is $\boldsymbol{x}(0)$?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}$, the first of the two points
The origin, since every coordinate is scaled by 0
$\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}$, since its weight becomes 1
The midpoint, at the centre of the joining segment

questions.question: An LP has optimal solutions $(8,0)$ and $(0,4)$. Which point is the convex combination $\tfrac{1}{4}(8,0)+\tfrac{3}{4}(0,4)$?
An LP has optimal solutions $A=(1,5)$ and $B=(5,1)$. Which point is guaranteed to be optimal by the convex combination property?
An LP has three optimal solutions $(8,0)$, $(0,8)$ and $(4,4)$. Which point is the combination with weights $0.5$, $0.25$ and $0.25$, in this order?

For the LP $\max 2x_s+2x_t$ subject to $2x_s+x_t\le100$, $x_s+x_t\le80$, $x_s\le40$, $x_s,x_t\ge0$, whose optimal corners are $(0,80)$ and $(20,60)$ with $z^*=160$, the point $(5,75)$ is written as $\alpha(0,80)+(1-\alpha)(20,60)$. What is $\alpha$?

For the LP $\max 2x_s+2x_t$ subject to $2x_s+x_t\le100$, $x_s+x_t\le80$, $x_s\le40$, $x_s,x_t\ge0$, whose optimal corners are $(0,80)$ and $(20,60)$ with $z^*=160$, which point is also an optimal solution?

$\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}$ is optimal for an LP with objective $3x_1+2x_2$, and $\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}$ is optimal for an LP with the same constraints but objective $2x_1+3x_2$. Is $\tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}+\tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}$ optimal for either LP?
options: Not necessarily; the proposition needs optima of the same LP.
Yes, for both LPs, since the average of feasible points is again feasible.
Yes, for both, provided $\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}$ and $\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}$ are corner points.
No, never: a mixture of optima of different LPs cannot be optimal.

questions.question: An LP has optimal value $z^*=160$. A point $\boldsymbol{x}$ has objective value exactly 160. When is $\boldsymbol{x}$ an optimal solution?
options: Always, because its value equals $z^*$.
Only when $\boldsymbol{x}$ is a corner point.
Only when every constraint holds with equality.
Exactly when $\boldsymbol{x}$ is feasible.

questions.question: Optimal solutions $\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol{x}^{(k)}$ of a maximization LP with objective $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ share the value $z^*$. Why does $\sum_j\alpha_j\boldsymbol{x}^{(j)}$, with $\alpha_j\ge0$ and $\sum_j\alpha_j=1$, also have value $z^*$?
options: By linearity its value averages values that all equal $z^*$.
Feasible combinations of optimal points always have value $z^*$.
Nonnegative weights cannot lower an objective.
The combination is again a corner of the region.

questions.question: An LP has optimal solutions $(5,0)$ and $(3,4)$, so every $(3+2\alpha,\,4-4\alpha)$ with $0\le\alpha\le1$ is optimal. A further requirement asks for $x_2=2$. Which optimal solution meets it?

In a maximization LP, $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ is optimal with value 20, and $\boldsymbol{y}$ is feasible with value 12. What is the value of $0.75\boldsymbol{x}^*+0.25\boldsymbol{y}$, and is that point optimal?
options: 20, as every convex combination is optimal
16, the average of the two values
18, so the mixed point is not optimal
12, the smaller of the two values

questions.question: A minimization LP has optimal production plans $(2,0,4)$ and $(0,3,2)$, both with cost 50. A manager uses 40% of the first plan and 60% of the second. Which plan results, and what is its cost?
On $0\le x\le2$ the function $f(x)=(x-1)^2$ takes its largest value 1 at both $x=0$ and $x=2$. What does their average $x=1$ show about the convex combination property?
options: Nothing; the property holds, since $[0,2]$ is an interval.
It fails because $0\le x\le2$ is not a set of linear constraints.
With a nonlinear objective, averaging optima can fail: $f(1)=0$.
It fails only because there are just two optimal points.

questions.question: In the proof that $\boldsymbol{x}=\sum_j\alpha_j\boldsymbol{x}^{(j)}$ satisfies a constraint $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\le b$ whenever each $\boldsymbol{x}^{(j)}$ does, where are the conditions $\alpha_j\ge0$ and $\sum_j\alpha_j=1$ used?
options: $\alpha_j\ge0$ keeps each scaled inequality; $\sum_j\alpha_j=1$ turns $\sum_j\alpha_jb$ into $b$.
Only $\sum_j\alpha_j=1$ is used; the signs of the weights play no role in the bound.
Only $\alpha_j\ge0$ is used; any nonnegative weights keep the constraint satisfied.
Neither is used for feasibility; both serve only to keep the objective value at $z^*$.

questions.question: For the LP $\max 2x_s+2x_t$ subject to $2x_s+x_t\le100$, $x_s+x_t\le80$, $x_s\le40$, $x_s,x_t\ge0$, whose optimal corners are $(0,80)$ and $(20,60)$ with $z^*=160$, a colleague notes that $(30,50)$ lies on the line $x_s+x_t=80$ through both optimal corners and has value 160, and calls it optimal. Writing $(30,50)=\alpha(0,80)+(1-\alpha)(20,60)$, what is wrong?
options: Nothing; every point on that line with value 160 is optimal.
Its value is not 160, so it cannot be optimal.
Its weight $1-\alpha=\tfrac{3}{2}$ is fine, as the weights still sum to 1.
It needs $\alpha=-\tfrac{1}{2}$ and violates $2x_s+x_t\le100$.

questions.question: The integer program $\max x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\le3$, $x_1\le2$, $x_2\le2$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer has optimal solutions $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$. What can be said about their average $(1.5,1.5)$?
options: It is optimal for the integer program, by the convex combination property.
It is not optimal because its value is lower than 3.
It has value 3 but is not feasible for the integer program.
It is not optimal because it violates $x_1+x_2\le3$.
